scenes.heading: Meiosis
scenes.sub: Why siblings are never exactly alike
scenes.say: Brothers and sisters with the same parents are never exactly alike, unless they're identical twins. Why? Because of meiosis, the cell division that makes gametes.

scenes.heading: What meiosis does
points: One diploid cell → four haploid cells
DNA copied once, cell divides twice
scenes.say: Meiosis turns one diploid cell into four haploid cells. It halves the chromosome number, so fertilisation restores it. DNA is copied once, but the cell divides twice. And it shuffles alleles, so every gamete is genetically different.

scenes.heading: Meiosis I vs meiosis II
scenes.say: Meiosis one splits the partners: homologous pairs line up together, then separate. That's what halves the chromosome number. Meiosis two splits the sisters: sister chromatids are pulled apart, much like mitosis. The result is four haploid cells.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Swap sandwich halves with a mate: new combinations
scenes.science: Crossing over swaps DNA between non-sister chromatids
scenes.breaks: Swapping with an identical sandwich changes nothing, just like a swap between identical sister chromatids.
scenes.say: You have a ham sandwich, and your mate has an egg one. Swap halves, and you each get a new combination. In prophase one, non-sister chromatids swap sections of DNA at chiasmata. That's crossing over. Swapping with an identical sandwich would change nothing, and the same goes for sister chromatids.

scenes.heading: Cut, shuffle, deal
scenes.say: Think of a deck of cards. Crossing over cuts and swaps pieces. Independent assortment shuffles whole chromosomes, because each pair lines up randomly at metaphase one. And random fertilisation deals which sperm meets which egg.

scenes.heading: Counting combinations
scenes.say: From independent assortment alone, the number of combinations is two to the power of n, where n is the haploid number. For humans, that's two to the twenty-three, about eight point four million. If a species has a diploid number of eight, n is four, so two to the four gives sixteen.
scenes.caption: From independent assortment alone, the number of combinations is 2ⁿ, where n is the haploid number. For humans, that's 2²³, about 8.4 million. If a species has 2n = 8, n is 4, so 2⁴ gives 16.

scenes.heading: Non-disjunction
points: Anaphase I error: all four gametes affected
scenes.say: Non-disjunction is when chromosomes fail to separate. One gamete gets an extra chromosome, and another is missing one. An error in anaphase one affects all four gametes. In anaphase two, two stay normal. If a gamete with an extra chromosome twenty-one is fertilised, the result is trisomy twenty-one.
scenes.caption: Non-disjunction is when chromosomes fail to separate. One gamete gets an extra chromosome, and another is missing one. An error in anaphase I affects all four gametes. In anaphase II, two stay normal. If a gamete with an extra chromosome 21 is fertilised, the result is trisomy 21.

points: Meiosis I splits partners; II splits sisters
scenes.say: Quick recap. Meiosis makes four genetically different haploid cells. Meiosis one splits the partners, meiosis two splits the sisters. Crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation create variation. Now try the practice questions!
